dagul_merevavah.en: His words are puzzling — what relevance do eleven hours have, since minchah ketanah begins from nine and a half hours? If Magen Avraham is stringent that one wait until the end of minchah time, then necessarily: if like the Rabbis, he waits until near evening; if like R' Yehuda, minchah time has already passed, for R' Yehuda's time is only until eleven hours less a quarter. But certainly hours before minchah gedolah — and so in Hagahot Ashiri chapter "ve'elu megalechim," and an incident with Rabbeinu Yaavetz, etc., who commanded to pray minchah gedolah after ten hours, etc.; and certainly it must be after six hours, since he wrote minchah gedolah — and in print vav was exchanged for yod; therefore the main point is that one prays minchah gedolah. I also saw Eliyah Rabbah noted this.

peri_megadim.he: יושבים עט״ז באבל אסור ע״ג כסא וספסל מדינא עי״ד שפ״ז וכאן ממנהגא ומקילין אחר חצות אבל בט״ז משמע דמדינא כל מצות הנהוגות באבל ובסיפא מסיים רחיצה כו׳ ולא ישיבת ספסל ש״מ אחר מצות שרי הא שאר דברים אסורים כל היום ומשמע אף ביה״ש עד צ״ה כאכילה ושתייה ות״ב ביה״ש שלו אסור. כ״ש מוצאי ט״ב עמ״א תקס״ב:

rabbi_akiva_eiger.he:
סעיף ד' בהג"ה וקורין בתורה כי תוליד מיהי תמהתי על שראיתי הנהוג שאומרים קדיש אחר שקרא השלישי בתורה קודם שאומרים ההפטרה הא מבואר דהמפטיר צריך לקרות בתורה תחלה שלא יהא כבוד ההפטרה ככבוד התורה לעלות בשביל ההפטרה לחוד אלא דמדינא השביעי הוא המפטיר דמפטר עולה למנין הקרואים. אלא כיון דמוסיפים בשבת (וכן ביו"ט יש דעות) עבדי' ככ"ע לקרות מנין הקרואים זולת המפטיר אבל עכ"פ המפטיר צריך שיקרא בתורה תחלה וא"כ אם מפסיקים בקדיש כשאומר אח"כ ההפטרה והוי כעולה להפטרה לחוד ויהי' הכרחי לעלות אחר לקרות בתורה ולהפטיר ומה"ט כ' המג"א סי' רפ"ב סט"ז אההי' דהתם יפטיר מי שעולה לז' ואל יאמר הקדיש אחריו וא"כ מה בין אם השביעי הוא המפטיר דאין מפסיקין בקדיש לקריאתו לאמירת ההפטרה ומה בין ט"ב דהשלישי הוא המפטיר שיאמרו קדיש ומצאתי במנהגים כתב כן לומר קדיש קודם אמירת ההפטרה וכן ראיתי בלבוש וכ' הטעם שלא לומר הקדיש קודם קריאת השלישי כיון דעדיין לא נגמר מנין הקרואים. עיי"ש אבל מ"מ אינו מעלה ארוכה על אמירת הקדיש בין קריאה לאמירת ההפטרה ולא מלאני לבי לבטל המנהג ותה"ל מצאתי היום בתשובת הר"י מינ"ץ שנשאל על מה אין נוהגים לומר קדיש בט"ב וכן ביוה"כ במנחה אחר קריאת השלישי קודם אמירת ההפטרה והשיב כדברים הנ"ל דא"א לומר הקדיש דהוי הפסק ויהיה הכרחי לעלות עוד לקרות בתורה ולהפטיר וזהו א"א עיי"ש הנראה דהמנהג היה שלא לומר הקדיש עד שעמד השואל אמאי א"א הקדיש ולענ"ד כך הוא מעיקר הדין לומר בט"ב הקדיש אחר אמירת ההפטרה דהקדיש קאי על קריאת התור' וההפטרה לא הוי הפסק כמ"ש המג"א סי' רפ"ב סקט"ו ובמנחה ביו"הכ הקדיש שאומרים מיד אחר הקריאה לפני התיבה קודם תפלת מנחה עולה על הקריאה ומה"ט הייתי נהוג בהיותי בק"ק פריד לאנד שהמנהג שבמנחה הולכים קצתם לבהכ"נס זוטא לקרות שם בתורה לומר קדיש אחר אמירת ההפטרה כיון דאין מתפללים שם מנחה והולכים לחזרה לבהכנ"ס הוי הפסק. ולא קאי הקדיש של תפלת מנחה על הקריאה וה"נ בט"ב שאומרים הקינות אחר הקריאה הוי הפסק הרבה וראוי לומר קדיש אחר קריאת ההפטרה:
מג"א סק"ה בשחרית משכימין. ע' בא"ר:

turei_zahav.he: משום דמקרי מועד. נ"ל דמותר לעשות הספד על חכם שמת ולישב על גבי קרקע בט"ב דהא בלא"ה מספידין כל הקדושים בו ביום ואפי' אחר חצו' דכולי יומא ההוא קבוע לבכי' והספד ולענין זה לא אשגחי' במה דקרוי מועד וכ"מ מדלא הזכירו איסור הספד בט"ב כמ"ש שאר דברים כנלע"ד:
turei_zahav.en: (b) Because it is called a festival. It appears to me it is permitted to eulogize a sage who died and to sit on the ground on Tisha B'Av, for otherwise all the righteous are eulogized on that day and even after chatzot, for that entire day is fixed for weeping and eulogy; and for this purpose we pay no attention to its being called a festival, and so from that they did not mention the prohibition of eulogy on Tisha B'Av as they mentioned other matters — as I wrote, so it appears to me.

kaf_hachayim.he: ה) שם בהגה. וכן עושין בקריאת איכה. ויפסוק בין כל פסוק מעט ובין כל איכה ואיכה יותר מעט ופסוק האחרון שבכל איכה אומר בקול רם. דרשות מהרי"ל ה' ט"ב בסדר התפלה. מ"א ריש הסי'. ומברך על מקרא מגילה טרם מתחיל איכה. דרשות מהרי"ל שם. לבוש. מ"א שם. עט"ז ח"א כלל קל"א או' כ"ג. ואפי' בדפוס וכתוב על נייר מברכין לבוש. מחה"ש. ובח"א שם כתב דוקא אם היא בקלף ובגלילה כדין מברכין. ובא"א ריש הסי' כתב אף כתוב בקלף אין לברך יעו"ש. ומיהו עיין לעיל סי' ת"ץ או' פ"א שהבאנו פלוגתא בזה והגם דק"ל היכא דאיכא פלוגתא בברכות אין לברך משום סב"ל כמ"ש לעיל סי' י"ח או ז' מ"מ במקום שכבר נהגו לברך לא חיישינן לסב"ל כמ"ש לעיל סי' י"ז או' ב' יעו"ש וא"כ כל מקום יעשה כמנהגו אך היכא דליכא מנהג אין לברך משום סב"ל:
kaf_hachayim.en: (ה) In the gloss there. And likewise they do when reading Eichah: they pause a little between each verse and more between each "Eichah," and the last verse in each Eichah they say in a loud voice. Derashot Maharil section 5 Tisha B'Av in order of prayer. Magen Avraham at the beginning of this siman. And one blesses on mikra megillah before beginning Eichah. Derashot Maharil there. Levush. Magen Avraham there. Otzar HaChaim volume 1 general rule 131 note 23. And even in print on paper they bless — Levush. Machatzit HaShekel. And in Chayei Adam there he wrote specifically if it is on parchment and rolled as required they bless. And in Orach Chaim at the beginning of this siman he wrote even written on parchment one does not bless — see there. However see above siman 559 note 81 where we brought a dispute in this; and although it is difficult — where there is a dispute in blessings one does not bless because of safeik berachot as written above siman 18 note 7 — nevertheless where they already practiced to bless we are not concerned for safeik berachot as written above siman 17 note 2 — see there; if so, everywhere one acts per custom, but where there is no custom one does not bless because of safeik berachot.

(כב) אסור לספר דבר - וכ"ש שרע עלי המעשה במה שקצת נוהגין קלות וזורקין זה לזה בביהכ"נ. ועון גדול הוא דאפילו שלא בט"ב אסור להראות קלות בביהכ"נ וכ"ש בט"ב ובשעת קינות שעם ישראל מקוננים על בית ד' שנחרב ועל עמו שנפזרו בכל העולם:

yad_ephraim.he: ס"ק ח' מותר לילך לבה"כ והשתא ניחא הכל וכן הוא בפסקי התוס' ועיין בתוס' שם דף כ"א וכמ"ש אא"ז מהרש"א ז"ל ודבריו צ"ע ולפענ"ד אפשר לפרש מ"ש התוס' וע"ז סומכין שבאין לבה"כ בט"ב לא קאי אאבלים רק אכל בני אדם שאף עפ"י שבמ"ב אבילים הם יכולין לבא לבה"כ והשתא ניחא הכל. אמנם מפסקי התו' וכן מהרא"ש נראה דקאי אאבלים ובתוס' א"א לפרש כמ"ש המג"א לקמן שהרי הביאו ראיה מזה שמותר להניח תפילין בט"ב כל זה כתבתי בגליון ובחדושים כתבתי לפרש דברי אא"ז מהרש"א שכפי פשוטו הוא תמוה ודוחק גדול ולענ"ד הדברים כפשטן לא קאי על אבילים שנכניס לבה"כ אלא על כל אדם שאם נאמר בט"ב הוי כתוך ג' לא היו רשאים ליכנס בט"ב לבה"כ דאבל תוך ג' א"י לילך לאבל אחר אף שגם הוא תוך ג' כמ"ש המ"א וא"ל דט"ב שכולם אבילים שאני דבר זה יש ללמוד ממה דאיתא שם במ"ק ריש דף ך"ג גבי נשיא שקורין שבעה בס"ת ויוצאין ופירש"י שאין מתפללין בבה"כ אלא כ"א ואחד מתפלל בביתו עכ"ל מבואר דאף שכולם אבלים כ"א מתפלל לעצמו וכן הוא במפרש שברי"ף אך בדברי הרא"ש איתא שהם מתפללין בבית האבל והב"י ביו"ד סי' שע"ד כ' בשם רש"י וה"ה אפשר לומר שברש"י שלפנינו ג"כ צ"ל בביתו של אבל אך לשון כ"א ואחד לא משמע כן ועכ"פ י"ל דהתוספות ס"ל דבכה"ג שהוא אבילות דחמיר כגון נשיא אף שכולם אבילים אין הולכים לבה"כ ומזה הוכיחו דט"ב הוי כאבילות דאחר ג' והטעם שהוא אבילות ישינה כמ"ש המג"א בשם בד"ה אך דברי הרא"ש בתענית א"א לפרש כן ומ"ש המג"א הוא דחוק מאוד ולכן נלע"ד דודאי לכאורה הך דינא דאבל הולך לבה"כ בט"ב כיון שט"ב הוא כאבל לאחר ג' הוא מלתא דפשיטא כיון שברייתא מפורשת דאחר ג' הולך לבית האבל וע"כ דאבילות דט"ב חלוק מאבילות דעלמא וסימן לדבר תפילין שאם היה דינו כאבילות דעלמא היה לו להיות כאבל ביום ראשון דאסור בתפילין וא"כ דכל מילי אין ללמוד ט"ב מאבל וי"ל דדוקא לאבל אחר הולך אחר ג' משא"כ בט"ב ולזה בא לומר דט"ב אין חלוק מאבל דאף שא"א לומר דהוי כאבל דיום ראשון לפי שהוא אבילות ישינה מכל מקום הוי כאבל מיום ג' ואילך ואין ראיה מתפילין דנהי דהוי כאבל אחר ג' מכ"מ מותר בתפילין ואין ראיה מתפילין לומר דט"ב קיל מאבילות דעלמא דגם אבל אחר ג' מותר בתפילין ולפי"ז מבוארים דברי הרא"ש היטב שאין כוונתו לומר דט"ב הוי כאחר ג' כדי ליתן טעם הליכה מבהכ"נ דזה פשיטא ליה אלא כותב דרך הנחה דט"ב הוי כאבל yad_ephraim.en: (ח) It is permitted to go to the synagogue and now everything fits; and so in the rulings of Tosafot; and see in Tosafot there daf 21 and as the Rosh wrote — his words require study; in my humble opinion one can explain what Tosafot wrote and on this they rely that those who come to synagogue on Tisha B'Av does not refer to mourners but to all people, for even though in Mishna Berurah they are mourners they may come to synagogue — and now everything fits. However from the rulings of Tosafot and Rosh it appears it refers to mourners, and in Tosafot one cannot explain as Magen Avraham wrote below since they brought proof from this that one may lay tefillin on Tisha B'Av — all this I wrote in the margin; in my novellae I wrote to explain the words of the Rosh that in the simple sense it is astounding and very forced; in my opinion the simple sense does not refer to mourners entering synagogue but to every person — that if we said on Tisha B'Av it is like within three [days of mourning] they would not be permitted to enter synagogue on Tisha B'Av to synagogue, for a mourner within three may not go to another mourner even if he too is within three as Magen Avraham wrote — but Tisha B'Av where all are mourners is different; one learns this from what is stated there in Moed Katan beginning daf 23 regarding a nasi whom they call seven in Scripture and they leave — Rashi explained they do not pray in synagogue but each one prays in his house — end of his words; it is clear that even though all are mourners each prays for himself, and so in the commentary of Rif; but in the words of Rosh it states they pray in the house of mourning, and Beit Yosef Yoreh Deah siman 374 wrote in the name of Rashi and likewise one could say in our Rashi it should read in the mourner's house; but the wording "each one and one" does not imply so; in any case one could say Tosafot hold that in such a case of mourning that is stringent, such as a nasi — even though all are mourners they do not go to synagogue, and from this they proved Tisha B'Av is like mourning after three days, and the reason is that it is mourning of a different kind as Magen Avraham wrote in the name of Biur HaGra — but the words of Rosh in Taanit cannot be explained thus, and what Magen Avraham wrote is very forced; therefore it appears to me that certainly the law that a mourner goes to synagogue on Tisha B'Av since Tisha B'Av is like a mourner after three is obvious, since the baraita explicitly states that after three one goes to the house of mourning — therefore mourning of Tisha B'Av differs from ordinary mourning, and a sign for this is tefillin: if its law were like ordinary mourning it would be like a mourner on the first day who is forbidden tefillin — if so one should not learn anything of Tisha B'Av from a mourner; one could say specifically to another mourner one goes after three, unlike Tisha B'Av; therefore it comes to say Tisha B'Av is not different from a mourner — even though one cannot say it is like a mourner on the first day because it is mourning of a different kind, nevertheless it is like a mourner from the third day onward, and there is no proof from tefillin — for although it is like a mourner after three, nevertheless tefillin are permitted, and there is no proof from tefillin to say Tisha B'Av is lighter than ordinary mourning, for a mourner after three is also permitted tefillin; and accordingly the words of Rosh are well explained — his intent is not to say Tisha B'Av is like after three in order to give a reason for going from synagogue, for that is obvious to him; rather he writes by way of premise that Tisha B'Av is like a mourner, but one should not grasp it as an ordinary mourner implying the first day when tefillin would be forbidden; therefore he explained his words that it is properly like a mourner except it is like a mourner after three, therefore tefillin are permitted; nevertheless going is permitted as going to another mourner which is not lighter than ordinary mourning after three. The reader will see this is clear in the intent of Rosh as I wrote; also in the intent of the Rosh it appears that even though they said what Tosafot wrote and from here they relied etc. on mourners after three — as also implied from Rosh's words, since mostly he copies from Tosafot — nevertheless what they wrote "and from his words we learn" etc. does not mean only in the wording "from here they relied" but hints at what Tosafot HaRav wrote at greater length from which this is proven; and it seems to me that there Tosafot HaRav wrote in the language of Rosh in Taanit, therefore they wrote "and from his words" etc.; and there is a difference regarding tefillin. Perhaps his intent in what he wrote that he came to answer his words — even for this law he did not need the permission because he is like after three, for if there were concern of within three all the more he would be permitted to go to synagogue — only therefore he used the words after three, which matters for tefillin: if we say it is like before three the law would be not to lay tefillin on the first day; and in truth Tosafot HaRav agrees tefillin are permitted on Tisha B'Av, therefore he used this premise that it is like after three even though for this law of going to synagogue there is no difference; and one could also say per what the Rav wrote — and I do not know if it is a good custom — and what is his doubt? It is obvious one may go to the house of mourning as taught explicitly in the baraita, implying for every mourner even after three, and all the more on Tisha B'Av where he holds it is like before three; and it must be that he holds Tisha B'Av is only like after three; and one might have thought that even though it is also after three he may not go, for a mourner after three may only go to a mourner more stringent than himself — but from the baraita's wording that states generally "he goes to a mourner" it implies even when he is after three, namely that they wrote "on this they relied" meaning on the implication of the baraita's language that implies one goes to a mourner like himself who is also after three; therefore he was uncertain and wrote he does not know if it is good custom — one could explain their intent thus; but what he wrote first seems more correct in my opinion, and in the intent of Maharsha I also explained, and here I abbreviated.

magen_avraham.en: But one who is in mourning. The Rosh writes: A baraisa teaches that during the first three days a mourner may not go to another mourner's house, but afterward he may go. Tishah B'Av is likewise treated like mourning after the first three days, and the mourner may go to the synagogue with the rest of the congregation, who are all like mourners. Beit HaBechirah writes that since the mourning of Tishah B'Av is for an ancient calamity, it is no more stringent than mourning after the first three days. This requires study. If the mourner himself is within his first three days, he may not visit another mourner even if that other mourner is beyond three days. Why, then, should Tishah B'Av be different? Conversely, if he is beyond his own first three days, he may visit even a mourner who is within three days, since there is greater reason to permit visiting one whose grief is intense. Rabbeinu Yerucham writes explicitly that only a mourner who is beyond three days may go to the synagogue; see there. It is known that his rulings are based upon the Rosh. The Tur, however, rules without qualification, implying that even within the first three days it is permitted, and this also appears from the Rosh in chapter 3 of Moed Katan. The explanation must therefore be as follows: Tishah B'Av is treated like mourning after three days. Just as an ordinary mourner may go out after three days, so too on Tishah B'Av one may go to the synagogue even during the first three days, because everyone is in mourning. This requires study. Terumas HaDeshen objects that at night a mourner may go out when necessary, as stated in Yoreh Deah 393. One may answer that this applies when he goes alone, whereas here, since he goes together with a group of people, it would be forbidden were it not for the reason that all of them are mourners. See siman 581.

A gloss explains that the word "shirt" means a cloak, not an undershirt. Maharam Tiktin writes that the reason is that an undershirt is a private matter, whereas a cloak is worn publicly, and public mourning does not apply on Shabbos. He himself, however, explains that the accepted ruling is the reverse: the cloak is forbidden because a conspicuous garment is treated more stringently on Tishah B'Av than during ordinary mourning, as stated in siman 554, while the undershirt is permitted. So states Mordechai. It therefore appears that the participants in a bris may wear a white shirt, as stated in siman 551 in the name of Mateh Moshe. This is also implied by Minhagim, which states that the participants in a bris wear white, though not completely white garments, and not on Shabbos Chazon, etc. This implies that Shabbos Chazon is not treated more stringently. Shabbos garments that are still new and whose pressing is noticeable may not be worn, as stated in siman 551:6. Maharil writes that after the bris they remove these garments.

magen_avraham.en:
And it was postponed, etc. If a bris occurs on Tishah B'Av itself, those involved complete the fast. [Beit Yosef] This is also implied by what is written in siman 558 in the name of Maharil. An objection was raised before Maharam Lublin from Eruvin, at the end of chapter 3. Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok said: Once Tishah B'Av fell on Shabbos and was postponed until Sunday. We fasted but did not complete the fast because it was our festival, meaning that the wood offering of his family was brought on the tenth of Av. The Gemara asks: The reason they did not complete it was that it was their festival, but on the eve of their festival they would complete it. This proves that one may complete a fast on Friday. The objection is as follows: This festival, had it coincided with Tishah B'Av, would not have displaced the fast, so certainly one should complete the fast on its eve. Shabbos, however, does displace Tishah B'Av when they coincide, so perhaps one should likewise not complete a fast on Friday. It must therefore be that even on their own festival they would not complete Tishah B'Av itself. How, then, could Beit Yosef rule that one completes the fast when a bris occurs on Tishah B'Av? He answered that the questioner indeed assumed that they would not complete the fast even on Tishah B'Av itself. The answer of the Gemara, however, was that a privately observed festival instituted by the Sages is different: since they fast for part of the day, they may complete the fast on its eve, but Tishah B'Av itself is not displaced by it. It appears to me that the Gemara's question contains an additional difficulty. According to the questioner's assumption that Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok did not follow Rabban Gamliel, why did they not complete the fast? Even on Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, and Purim one completes a fast, as stated in siman 472:2, all the more so on their private festival. The necessary conclusion is that because Tishah B'Av had been postponed from its proper date, it was treated more leniently. If, however, he followed Rabban Gamliel, who holds that one never completes a fast on the eve of a festival, then they should not have completed any ordinary Tishah B'Av either. The Gemara answers that a festival instituted by the Sages is different, etc. Accordingly, since we do not follow Rabban Gamliel and rule that even on Rosh Chodesh one fasts and completes the fast, all the more so on a private festival. Only a postponed Tishah B'Av is treated leniently. Similarly, when a communal fast is decreed, everyone must complete it. See siman 568:2 and Taanis 12. Knesses HaGedolah writes that one should nevertheless not make a festive meal. The present custom is to complete the fast even when one of the four fasts has been postponed. Radbaz likewise rules this way in part 2, siman 35. When the bris takes place after midday, one may not be lenient even on one of the four fasts, unless the fast was postponed. Rabbi Shlomo HaLevi writes that a bridegroom on a communal fast does not complete his fast, even though he could have postponed the wedding, unlike the case of a bris. During the seven days of celebration, however, he does complete the fast. This applies in a place where the custom is not to fast on the wedding day. Knesses HaGedolah records this ruling. Nowadays the widespread custom is that most wedding meals are held at night. Accordingly, there is no basis for leniency during the daytime fast.

yad_ephraim.en: There, per the view of the questioner that he does not act, etc. — meaning the Talmud there comes to prove that he does not act like Rabbenu Gershom; for if he acted like Rabbenu Gershom who holds on Tisha B'Av that falls on erev Shabbat they do not complete — if so on every Tisha B'Av they would not need to complete; and per this view the questioner's view is that granted if he does not act like Rabbenu Gershom it is not surprising that on every Tisha B'Av they completed, for they do not heed Yom Tov at all — even on Rosh Chodesh, etc. they complete; only because it was deferred they are lenient; not so if one says he acts like Rabbenu Gershom — if so even when not deferred they do not complete on erev Shabbat; and for us likewise if our Yom Tov is on Tisha B'Av they do not complete — if so on every Tisha B'Av they should not have completed, for their Yom Tov is on it; per the view of the questioner then if he acts like Rabbenu Gershom indeed if their Yom Tov fell on Tisha B'Av itself they also would not complete, per the reasoning of the questioner in Maharam; and if so the same on Yom Tov — he should not have completed like on Shabbat; therefore it answers that even Rabbenu Gershom agrees on Yom Tov that their words, etc. And per this for us who rule not like Rabbenu Gershom we state simply like the questioner's view that on our sixth day too one should be stringent, for it is not better than Rosh Chodesh — only when deferred there is to be lenient. And per the girsa before us in Magen Avraham that he challenged another question — it appears to me some words are missing in Magen Avraham that he challenged another question, and from where to distinguish between deferred or not? For it was necessary to say there that it was deferred because their Yom Tov was the tenth of Av; therefore it appears certainly one must distinguish in this. Per the view of the questioner, etc., as should be — and meaning the questioner there in responsum of Maharam siman 98 challenged there on what Beit Yosef wrote proof that deferred specifically, from that it says "and it was deferred" and does not say simply "and we fasted on Tisha B'Av and did not complete it," etc.; and on this it says it was necessary to say it was deferred since their Yom Tov was the tenth of Av; and for this Magen Avraham wrote the proof is thus: behold the questioner comes to prove he does not act like Rabbenu Gershom — it should have stated simply "and we fasted on Tisha B'Av and did not complete it," etc.; rather necessarily he does not act like Rabbenu Gershom; if so what that they did not complete it is because when deferred they are lenient. And per this for us who rule not like Rabbenu Gershom one is lenient only when deferred. And the view of the questioner that he should not have completed even without deferral — this is if he acts like Rabbenu Gershom; for then since it fell on their Yom Tov itself they complete; for us like if the ninth of Av fell on Rosh Chodesh on Chanukah and Purim — Rabbenu Gershom holds that even though they do not interrupt, nevertheless they do not complete; and so he holds on Tisha B'Av that falls on erev Shabbat; if so also on their Yom Tov they do not complete; and if so the same if it fell on Yom Tov like when it fell on erev Shabbat that they do not complete for Rabbenu Gershom; not so for us who do not rule like him — even on Yom Tov itself they do not defer unless it was deferred, per the questioner's view that he does not act like Rabbenu Gershom; and one need not answer Maharam that specifically for the reason they answered thus. And see below siman 572 in Magen Avraham there and on what is written on Taz there:
